newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 2.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- BLAIR VOWS TO BRING IN 'AGE OF ACHIEVEMENT'

Speaking at the Labour party annual conference in Blackpool, leader Tony Blair has set out a series of 10 pledges that he is committing Labour to achieving should it secure victory in the next general election. Speaking of his expectation of an "age of achievement" under Labour, Blair committed his party to a series of goals, including boosting spending on education, reducing youth unemployment by half, and turning Britain into "the skill superpower of the world".
-- HOUSE OF FRASER IN 50 MILLION STG REVAMP

House of Fraser has announced that as a result of plans to shut between 5 and 10 of its 51 retail outlets, it will be making provision of 50 million stg. The provision is expected to result in the company suffering a full-year loss. The company also announced that it would be embarking on a major overhaul of its remaining stores in an effort to reverse falling profits and market loss. The plans were met with a certain degree of scepticism and shares in the company fell in response.
-- IMPERIAL TOBACCO SHARES MAKE STRONG DEBUT

Shares in Imperial Tobacco, demerged from the Hanson conglomerate, are reported to have performed well on their first day of trading, closing up 18.5p to 393p. There was particularly strong demand for shares in London where fund managers have been impressed by the company's cash flow. The presence of the company on the FTSE 100, having replaced Southern Electric, was also seen as a factor in the strong demand.
-- EUROTUNNEL CLOSE TO DEBT DEAL

Sources at Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel have expressed optimism that an agreement can be reached in the near future with its lender banks on a refinancing deal that could prevent the company being placed in administration by a French court. The company, which has debts of some 8.8 billion stg, has been attempting for more than a year to restructure this gearing and recently missed a deadline for the securing of agreement on the issue.
-- CHIRAC ANGERS ITALY OVER SINGLE CURRENCY

A political row has broken out between Rome and Paris after the French president Jacques Chirac expressed skepticism about Italy's ability to meet the Maastricht criteria for participation in the single European currency. The French ambassador was summoned by Italian PM Romano Prodi, who reacted angrily to suggestions that his country might not be among the first wave of participants. However, Chirac has since distanced himself from the initial allegations, raising hopes that a Wednesday Franco-Italian summit would proceed as planned.
-- ROVER TO INVEST 400 MILLION STG IN MINI OF THE FUTURE

Rover Group, now owned by German auto giant BMW, has announced that it is to invest some 400 million stg in the production of a successor to its veteran Mini. It is anticipated that the new car, which will be bigger than the current model, will go on sale in 2001. The engine for the vehicle is to be produced at a plant in South America being jointly developed by BMW and Chrysler. The rest of the car, however, will remain British and is expected to be built at Rover's facility at Longbridge.
-- CONSORTIUM IN 15-YEAR DEAL TO TRAIN FORCES' HELICOPTER PILOTS

A 15-year, 400 million stg contract to train helicopter pilots for the British armed forces has been secured by a consortium including Cobham, SERCo and Bristow Helicopter. The group will supply as well as maintain 47 helicopters and will undertake the training of an estimated 230 aircrew each year at a facility in Shropshire. As part of the contract, 38 Squirrel helicopters are to be purchased from Eurocopter, a joint venture involving Aerospatiale and Daimler Benz Aerospace.
-- US-EU AVIATION TALKS SETBACK

Efforts by the European Union and the US to reach agreement on the issue of aviation rights have suffered a setback with the US noting that the negotiations were unlikely to achieve concrete results. Speaking in Prague, US assistant secretary for aviation, Charles Hunnicut, noted that the insistence by the European Commission that the talks be approached in two stages was likely to prove and obstacle to accord on liberalisation of air traffic.
-- BELGIUM BUDGET FOR MONETARY UNION

The Belgian government has detailed the provisions of its budget for 1997. The package seeks to prepare the country for participation in the single European currency by reducing both the budget deficit and the level of government debt. While the country's debt is currently 127 percent of GDP, PM Dehaene expressed confidence that even a small reduction in light of other measures would be enough to convince its EU partners that the level was on a downward trend. The Maastricht target for government debt is currently 60 percent of GDP.
-- EU GOES TO WTO OVER CUBA LAW

The European Union is asking the World Trade Organisation to rule that the US Helms-Burton Act, which seeks to isolate Cuba economically and threatens foreign trade partners with sanctions, breaches international trade regulations. The decision is expected to heighten tension between the EU and the US, which had said that such a move would be viewed as provocative. European trade commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has noted that the appeal to the WTO demonstrates the capacity of the EU to defend itself.
